title: The Dragon Within and the Hardened Heart
english: The face that he put on: who is able to expose it? Who is able to uncover it and show what the dragon is within? And a little further on: I ran back to the memory of the sacred writings set down in this God-inspired book of Job, where, as in a bodily figure, he sketches what is exceedingly formless and many-sided and hidden in the schemes, and in the shedding of the outward masks, of the devil, the author of evil, and of the wicked demons. For it says: “Who will uncover the face of his garment?” (Job 41:13).

And since the roots of this variety that shows on the outside rise up as from some depth of unseen wickedness, these words too are added to what has been said: “Who will uncover the face of his garment?” That is: who is able to enter into the thoughts of his heart, since they are folded up together?

“It will not be shaken. His heart is set fast like a stone, and it stands like an anvil that cannot be beaten out” (Job 41:23-24). His heart, it says, has turned to stone and cannot be beaten out; he is wholly dried hard and headstrong. He is not beaten out, he does not follow reason, he does not yield; he is hard, unmalleable, unyielding. And if anyone has drawn power from the devil, he too has the heart of this dragon, unmalleable and not to be beaten out. But if anyone is gold, following the word, he yields to the goldsmith's art until he becomes a leaf of gold and receives the impressions of the letters of God, in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory to the ages of ages. Amen.

“And the Lord gave Job double all that he had before, for doubling” (Job 42:10). “And the Lord blessed the last days of Job more than the first; and his livestock were fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen” (Job 42:12). “And seven sons and three daughters are born to him” (Job 42:13). title: Double Blessings After Suffering
english: … stroke, as the sacred writing says, then his children too ought to have been doubled. Look at the livestock: he had, it says, fourteen thousand sheep, for at the beginning he had seven thousand (Job 1:3); six thousand camels, for at the beginning he had three thousand; a thousand yoke of oxen, for at first there were five hundred. The same holds for the grazing asses. Yet seven sons and three daughters, it says, are born to him, as many as there were before (Job 1:2). But there ought to have been fourteen sons and six daughters, so that they would be double the children he lost. We say, then, that the sheep and the livestock were lost, but the sons and the daughters died; they were not lost. So God gave him as many children again, so that in the resurrection he would have them double; and so God has made him the father of twice as many children as he was father of before. But if the soul were extinguished after death, and the resurrection were not real, he would have had to be given fourteen sons and six daughters. That is why Scripture has reverently kept to the statement that he received seven sons. For if fourteen sons and six daughters had been born to him, with the teaching on the resurrection still standing, the children given to him would not be double but triple what they were at first.

“And Job lived after the stroke a hundred and seventy years, and all the years he lived were two hundred and forty” (Job 42:16). How is Job understood to have lived a hundred and seventy years after the stroke, when the whole of his life came to two hundred and forty-eight years? We say, then, reckoning closely, that since he received all his goods back double, if he also received back double the years of his former prosperity, this is how the count should be made. He lived seventy-seven years in his former plenty, and from the time he received the stroke he remained in suffering fourteen years. So “after the stroke” must be understood to mean not from when the stroke ceased but from when it began. And after the fourteen years, the time of his disease, …

title: Duration of Job's Life and Resurrection
english: … he lived another hundred and fifty-six years. For since the years of his former prosperity were seventy-eight, the double time of his later good fortune comes to a hundred and fifty-six years; and when the fourteen years of the stroke are added before them, the total is a hundred and seventy years. So he is found to have lived a hundred and seventy years after the stroke, that is, from the time the stroke was brought on him, as Scripture says. In this way the double repayment of his plenty is also kept. To sum up, then, you will count like this: he lived in wealth and in the blessing of children seventy-eight years; in the loss of everything and the affliction of his body, fourteen years; in his second good fortune, a hundred and fifty-six years; so that the whole time of his life is two hundred and forty-eight years, as the sacred book about him says.

“And Job died, old and full of days” (Job 42:17). “And it is written that he will rise again with those whom the Lord raises up.” Aquila and Symmachus, on reaching this point, ended the book, since they follow the Hebrew; but Theodotion ends it together with the Seventy, leaving nothing out, neither the time nor the life. It is written that he will rise again with those whom the Lord raises up: the righteous, clearly. For “the ungodly,” it says, “will not rise in judgement, nor sinners in the council of the righteous” (Psalm 1:5). We accept these words too, even if not as belonging to the whole fabric of the book, yet as if one of the saints had woven them into it; still, we accept all of it, since we have received the book in this form from the fathers.

“This one is translated from the Syriac book.” Here he calls the language of the Hebrews Syriac, since most people also call Judea Syria and call the Palestinians Syrians. Herodotus the historian, too, says: “The Indians, the Egyptians, the Arabs and the Syrians in Palestine are circumcised”; it is the Jews that they call by this name.

added_allusions.reason: 'It is written that he will rise again with those whom the Lord raises up' and 'This one is translated from the Syriac book' are the Septuagint's additions after Job 42:17; the KJV verse does not contain them, so no reference is printed beside them.
